title: PJM Proposes Framework To Connect Data Centers Without Compromising Reliability, Affordability
date_evidence: # PJM Proposes Framework To Connect Data Centers Without Compromising Reliability, Affordability                    August 13, 2026
key_claim: PJM filed with FERC on 13 August 2026 a proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) under which new Large Load customers that do not bring their own new capacity would have demand reduced or transferred during emergencies ahead of traditional consumers, including residential consumers, and ahead of Load Management customers who are paid in advance to reduce use. PJM would create a Large Load Registry, and from the 2029/2030 capacity auction new Large Loads without their own supply would not be counted when calculating future power needs to be procured. Of 32 GW of forecast demand growth between 2024 and 2030, 30 GW is attributed to data centres.
frame_summary: PJM is arguing that new large loads which do not bring matching new generation should hold a lower service priority than existing consumers, so that data centre growth can be connected quickly without transferring reliability risk or cost onto households.
verbatim_quote: Of 32 GW of growth in forecasted electricity demand between 2024 and 2030, 30 GW is attributed to data centers.
verbatim_list: a new emergency procedure would notify utilities to reduce or transfer the electricity demand from new Large Load customers ahead of any action that would serve to shut off traditional consumers, including residential consumers
This curtailment of service would come before calling on Load Management customers, who are paid in advance to reduce their electricity use when directed by PJM in emergencies.

PJM proposes that beginning with the 2029/2030 capacity auction, new Large Loads that do not bring their own new supply to the system will not be included when calculating the future power needs to be procured in those auctions.
notes: PJM is the RTO itself; treated as Tier 1 primary for its own filing. title: Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System (Docket No. RM26-4-000)
date_evidence: This page was last updated on July 22, 2026

Large loads are defined for the docket as electricity demand greater than 20 MW.

title: Commissioner Rosner's Remarks on the Large Load Show Cause Orders, E-7 to E-12, June 18, 2026 Open Meeting
date_evidence: Commissioner Rosner's Remarks on the Large Load Show Cause Orders, E-7 to E-12 | June 18, 2026 Open Meeting
key_claim: At the 18 June 2026 open meeting FERC issued show cause orders E-7 to E-12 covering the large load dockets. The Commission's own framing is that the large loads seeking to connect today are larger, sometimes by orders of magnitude, and more concentrated than traditional load growth.
frame_summary: FERC is arguing that the scale and concentration of new large loads is a generational change that existing transmission tariffs were not written for, which is why the Commission is compelling every RTO to justify or rewrite them at once.

title: Understanding FERC's Large Load Orders
date_evidence: [Brief](https://rmi.org/resource-types/brief/) July 6, 2026 # Understanding FERC's Large Load Orders
key_claim: In June 2026 FERC issued show cause orders to six RTOs/ISOs (PJM, MISO, SPP, CAISO, ISO-NE, NYISO) under section 206 of the Federal Power Act, finding existing tariffs unjust and unreasonable. Among five reform categories, FERC ordered the RTOs to create three new transmission services previously described in PJM's co-location proceeding: interim network integration transmission service, non-firm contract demand service, and firm contract demand service. FERC suggested defining a large load as a new facility over 50 MW seeking transmission service above 69 kV.
frame_summary: RMI is arguing that FERC's June orders convert large-load interconnection from an ad hoc negotiation into a standardised set of transmission products in which curtailability is an explicit, priced tier of service.
verbatim_quote: new large loads that can be curtailed when transmission capacity is constrained
verbatim_list: Non-firm contract demand service: LSEs can reserve non-firm transmission service to serve new large loads that can be curtailed when transmission capacity is constrained. This permanent product is curtailed before firm transmission service.
FERC suggested defining a large load as a new facility over 50 MW, seeking transmission service above 69 kV, and not part of co-located arrangements.
In June of 2026, FERC issued separate orders to six regional grid operators (RTOs/ISOs) to initiate show cause proceedings pursuant to section 206 of the Federal Power Act.

Firm contract demand service: LSEs can reserve a contracted amount of firm transmission service for a portion of a large load facility's load; this product receives equal prioritization as other firm transmission services.

title: Beyond Scalar Flexibility: From Eligible AI Workloads to Dependable Load Relief
key_claim: Using 4,439 hourly power observations reconstructed from a 185-day production trace of 155,410 GPUs, the authors find median facility demand of 55.8 MW and immediate eligible curtailment averaging 3.55 MW, which is 12.1% of workload power and 6.35% of median facility power. Relief that is 95% available falls from 2.51 MW at one hour to 1.95 MW at 24 hours, a mean-calibrated single percentage overstates these quantities by 17%, 25% and 47%, and the production scheduler exposes almost no additional delay-based capacity.
frame_summary: The authors are arguing that a single flexibility percentage is the wrong unit of account for AI load, and that dependable relief must be specified by duration, reliability, portfolio and realisability terms if it is to be written into interconnection and demand-response contracts.
verbatim_quote: 4,439 hourly power observations from a 185-day trace of 155,410 GPUs
verbatim_list: We reconstruct 4,439 hourly power observations from a 185-day trace of 155,410 GPUs and derive a workload-semantic flexibility envelope.

title: Shift or curtail? How much data-center flexibility is worth in different power systems
key_claim: The authors classify data-centre load as firm, flexible or interruptible and embed each class in capacity expansion models for PJM and Korea. In PJM the value of flexibility is spatial: shifting workloads between zones reduces system cost by 6% in 2028 and 19% in 2038, avoiding 4.4 GW and 8.9 GW of gas and nuclear generation. In Korea the value is temporal. In both systems, realistic event-shape limits diminish the value of curtailment.
frame_summary: The authors are arguing that data-centre flexibility has no single value, because what a flexible megawatt is worth depends on the host grid's characteristics and policy objectives, which means procurement design rather than technology determines the payoff.

title: The Importance of Data Center Flexibility in Southeast Asia
key_claim: RMI models Peninsular Malaysia and finds that projected new data centre demand ranges from 1.1 GW to 7.7 GW by 2030 against roughly 20 GW of peak demand today, and that treating that load as 24/7 firm implies around 3 GW of new gas capacity. If data centres shift load during about 600 hours a year, roughly 6.8% of the time, Malaysia may avoid or defer up to 800 MW of gas. RMI's modelling assumes a maximum flexibility of 40% load reduction. Less than half of contracted Malaysian data centre demand has materialised to date.
frame_summary: RMI is arguing that Southeast Asian regulators should make flexibility the price of faster interconnection now, because planning for data centres as firm round-the-clock load would lock in gas capacity whose stranded cost falls on ratepayers.
verbatim_quote: Under the load shifting scenario, if data centers can shift load during ~600 hours (~6.8% of the time), Malaysia may avoid or defer up to 800 MW of gas, or 0.16 MW per MW of data center load.
verbatim_list: RMI assumed a maximum flexibility of 40% reduction of load, while generally keeping load reductions to roughly 5% and 20% in the peak shaving and load shifting scenarios, respectively.
In Malaysia, less than half of contracted data center demand has materialized to date, due to low utilization and speculative applications

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) has recently implemented a "Batch Zero" framework, allowing facilities of 75 MW and above to get prioritized in the interconnection queue by registering as provisional controllable load resources.

title: Data centers are ready to negotiate flexibility for speed
key_claim: Hyperscalers and utilities have converged on trading flexibility for speed to power but lack common operating guidelines. EPRI demonstrations have delivered flexibility of up to 40%, and modelling of training and inference workloads suggests 18% to 55% flexibility relative to average power consumption while meeting quality of service requirements. Silicon Valley Power's chief operating officer says the utility requires full control of the load-side breaker as the condition of faster interconnection.
frame_summary: Utility Dive is arguing that the technical case for data centre flexibility is now settled and the binding constraint has moved to contract: who holds operational control of the load, and on what standardised terms.
verbatim_quote: Training and inference workloads “can offer between 18% and 55% flexibility relative to their average power consumption” and still meet quality of service requirements, modeling found.
verbatim_list: EPRI’s demonstrations have delivered flexibility of up to 40%, but future AI infrastructure with designed-in flexibility can “materially” expand that, Shah said.
Just a 1% to 2% reduction in data center peak demand can reduce electricity rates 0.5% to 2.8% and protect reliability
